items.t: Databricks’ new AI agent tells CEO Ali Ghodsi the unvarnished truth
items.x: At 12,000 employees, AI Ghodsi is the first to admit that he can't know everyone and that they are unlikely to confess the things that go wrong to him. But he doesn't need them to. He uses Databricks' newly revised Genie agent for that.
items.xd:
Databricks has released an updated version of its AI agent, Genie, which can now handle multi-step jobs that take a long time to finish. It works using an ontology that Databricks built, which gives Genie the context it needs from the information customers store on the Databricks platform.

According to the company, corporate leaders can assign Genie a wide range of tasks, and it will complete them without supervision. To show how it works, Databricks CEO Ali Ghodsi walked a TechCrunch reporter through how he uses the agent inside the company, rather than giving a standard product demo.

Ghodsi showed how Genie analyzed the parts of an employee satisfaction survey where the company scored poorly. He also showed how it helped him evaluate fixes that some executives had suggested for those low scores, and how it helped him decide which ones to discard. In another example, Genie summarized a sales pitch to a prospect that had gone badly, including the features the prospect said it needed before buying.

Genie also helped Ghodsi prepare for a podcast interview by reviewing his past appearances and drafting likely questions. During the conversation with the reporter, he had it suggest what he should say, and the advice was reasonable.

The most interesting use, according to the article, was that Ghodsi used Genie to find problems he is unlikely to hear about as a senior leader. He referred to Dunbar's number, the idea that humans can maintain stable relationships with about 150 people. In a small startup, a CEO knows everyone and gets honest negative news directly, but at a company with 12,000 employees, Ghodsi admits he cannot know everyone, and employees may not share bad news such as a failed sales call or a likely-to-fail HR idea. Ghodsi said that any company with more than 150 employees could get value from this kind of agent.

Databricks calls this practice of using its own product dogfooding. The company is now promoting Genie as an always-on agent for business leaders. Ghodsi says he also uses it in his personal life and prefers it to alternatives such as OpenClaw, Instinct, or Muse, which he considers less secure. He believes Genie can do for business work what AI agents and harnesses are doing for programmers. A harness is the software that wraps around an AI model and lets it use tools.

On the concern that agents could drive up corporate AI costs, Ghodsi said companies can control spending with Databricks' Unity Gateway product. It lets companies set usage limits and switch to cheaper open-weight models.

items.t: ChatGPT is getting verified AI ‘Business Agents’
items.x: ChatGPT is going to let you chat with verified "Business Agents" that represent a brand to help you with things like comparison shopping. The feature, available first to "eligible" e-commerce and online service businesses in the US, is launching as part of a suite of business-focused features in ChatGPT being announced today in beta. You […]
items.xd:
ChatGPT will soon let you chat with verified "Business Agents" that represent a brand and can help with things like comparison shopping. The feature is launching first for "eligible" e-commerce and online service businesses in the US, as part of a set of business-focused ChatGPT features announced today in beta.

If a business that has created one shows up in a ChatGPT response, you can start talking with its Business Agent. While chatting, you can ask about a business's offerings and follow-up questions, such as how two different products differ. Businesses can set the agent's instructions and provide business context so it knows how to respond.

Chats with Business Agents are clearly labeled and kept separate from your main ChatGPT conversation, OpenAI says. To show that an agent really represents the business, companies can claim their organization and get verified through a feature called Business Hub. OpenAI isn't sharing specifics about its verification methods, because different businesses use different methods, according to VP of monetization Benji Shomair.

Business Hub also gives companies insights, such as how often they are mentioned in ChatGPT responses and the top "discovery topics" where their business appears.

OpenAI says today's announcement is an early step in bringing businesses more deeply into ChatGPT. The company says it is starting with the basics: accurate business information, useful insights, and conversations that help people make informed decisions. OpenAI plans to explore more ways for businesses to connect with customers, directly or through agents, in ChatGPT and beyond.

items.t: eBay appears to have shut the door on third-party AI agents
items.x: eBay appears to have blocked AI agents, including Meta's Muse, from browsing on the platform - the latest speed bump in the AI agent race. A reader tells The Verge that for several weeks he's had his Muse agent browse and curate a daily digest of watches for sale on platforms like eBay, including a […]
items.xd:
eBay appears to have blocked AI agents, including Meta's Muse, from browsing its site. This is the latest obstacle in the race to build AI agents that can shop for people.

A reader told The Verge that for several weeks he had used his Muse agent to browse eBay and other platforms and build a daily list of watches for sale. The list included links, prices, shipping details, and notes about each watch's condition or style. This weekend, however, Muse could not pull any links or details from eBay and said it was blocked from the site. When The Verge tried to repeat the experience with other searches, it sometimes found that Muse pointed users to outside websites that copied eBay listings.

Companies often present shopping as a area where AI agents can help people, for example by booking travel, finding deals, or buying things for them. Yet retailers keep blocking these agents from their sites, which raises doubts about how useful they can be.

eBay had already changed its user agreement to ban tools such as "buy-for-me agents" and "LLM-driven bots" that place orders without a person reviewing them. Until recently, though, agents like Muse could still browse the site and collect listings.

An eBay spokesperson, Sybille St. Arromand, said AI is becoming part of the way eBay helps people discover, personalize, and sell items. She would not say directly whether eBay had recently added new limits on AI agents. She said eBay takes a selective approach to third-party access and has restricted agents in some cases, including unauthorized scraping and training on its data.

She also said eBay is in talks with possible partners and is looking for ways third-party agents could help new customers find its inventory. The company's focus, she said, is protecting the trusted experience that buyers and sellers expect from eBay.

Retailers differ in how comfortable they are with outside agents. Amazon blocks external agents from browsing or shopping entirely. Target allows agents to browse in some cases but blocks them in others. Shopify has opened its catalog of a billion listings so shoppers can set up agents to buy items for them.

Agents could change online shopping a great deal, partly because retail sites were built for human shoppers, not swarms of bots. The Verge found in October that someone could use Muse to tie up product listings on The RealReal, a secondhand designer consignment site, by having an agent keep adding an item to the user's cart. The RealReal changed its bot system after The Verge reported on the problem.

It is still unclear how common agent-based shopping really is. Uber said it completed only four rides booked through third-party agents in the third quarter, and only around 500 Uber Eats orders during the week of Halloween. DoorDash said it completed only "several hundred" orders placed through third-party agents. It reported 993 million total orders last quarter.

items.t: Google releases Gemini 4 Carbon with agent ‘swarm’ feature
items.x: Google is rolling out its latest AI model, Gemini 4 Carbon, to the general public after releasing it to a select group of "cybersecurity defenders" two weeks ago. Google claims Carbon is its "strongest model" yet, and capable of competing with the very best systems from Anthropic and OpenAI. Google says Gemini 4 Carbon "pushes […]
items.xd:
Google has released its newest AI model, Gemini 4 Carbon, to the general public. Two weeks ago, it was only available to a select group of "cybersecurity defenders."

Google says Carbon is its strongest model so far and can compete with the best systems from Anthropic and OpenAI. It also says Carbon goes further than Argon, the company's other frontier model, which launched last month.

Google still expects Argon to be the better choice for most software engineering and knowledge work. Carbon, however, is designed for harder tasks that test how intelligent a model can be, such as complex, multi-step coding and open-ended scientific research.

Google is also previewing a "swarm" feature on Antigravity, its platform for building with AI agents. The feature lets a user turn one prompt into a coordinated team of agents, which Google highlights as useful for long projects.

Carbon is available starting today through the Gemini API in Google AI Studio and Gemini for business, for all paying developers and enterprises. It is also open to all Google AI Ultra subscribers in the Gemini app, AI Mode in Search, and Antigravity. Google has not said when or whether lower-tier subscribers or free users will get access.

Carbon is priced aggressively, as Argon was. It launches at an introductory price of $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens. That is about a fifth the cost of OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra and a quarter the cost of Anthropic's Fable 5.2, which launched yesterday. Those introductory prices will double at the end of November, but Carbon would still be much cheaper per token than rival frontier models. Cost per token does not always reflect the final cost, since models can use different numbers of tokens for the same task.

Google's benchmark results, released when Carbon was first announced, place it among the most powerful models on the market across most measures, behind Fable 5.2. Companies can choose benchmark results that show their tools in the best light, so these numbers should be read with that in mind.

The release comes soon after Argon and marks a strong return for Google at the front of AI research. For months, the frontier race appeared to be between only Anthropic and OpenAI.

items.t: Meta’s AI agent Muse lands on Apple Watch and Android Wear OS
items.x: Users can now interact with Meta’s AI assistant through voice calls, text messages, or dictation on their Apple Watch.
items.xd:
Meta is bringing its Muse AI agent to Apple Watch and Wear OS, the Android smartwatch system, the company announced on Monday. Users can now talk to Meta's AI assistant through voice calls, text messages, or dictation right on their smartwatch.

This watch launch comes just a month after Meta released a dedicated iPad app for Muse. The assistant first appeared on the App Store in September, and its spread to Apple devices shows Meta's growing plans for its consumer AI product.

Muse is one of many consumer AI agents competing for users' attention. Like its rivals, it can connect to a user's accounts to manage email, meetings, and bills, and it can also book reservations, order groceries, set goals, and make purchases.

Users can customize their Muse avatar, changing it to look like a person, an animal, or another kind of character.

Muse is still new, but Meta has moved quickly to add features. A few days ago, Meta launched Spaces, a new way to communicate and work with Muse. Spaces are focused conversations about specific topics, which Meta calls "custom experiences" because they are mini apps built on the fly. They appear in the sidebar of the Muse interface, where the AI works toward a particular goal for the user.

Last week, Meta let users in the U.S. video chat with their Muse AI avatar. Meta says the avatar uses "subtle expressions and gestures" that match the tone and context of the conversation as it speaks. Muse cannot actually see users, but it can hear them and respond in real time.

Soon after launch, Muse became one of just 12 mobile apps to pass 10 million U.S. downloads in its first 40 days on the App Store. Only 11 other apps have reached that milestone, and Meta's Threads was the most recent, in July 2023.

items.t: Adobe is going all in on agentic AI
items.x: Adobe is committing itself to the notion that chatbots and AI agents could be your next design assistant, or even automate creative workflows and repetitive tasks on your behalf. Some of the tools and features announced today at Adobe's Max conference in Miami, Florida, include allowing your preferred third-party AI agents to access and change […]
items.xd:
Adobe is betting that AI chatbots and agents will become a regular part of how people design and create. It could act as a design assistant or handle creative workflows and repetitive tasks for you. The company announced several of these tools and features at its Max conference in Miami, Florida.

One change lets the AI agents you already use, such as those from OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic, work directly inside Adobe's Creative Cloud apps. Local integrations for Photoshop, Illustrator, Premiere, and After Effects were previewed, and these agents can make direct changes to project files stored on your computer.

You can step in at any time to fix or adjust the agent's work. All layers, vectors, bins, and sequences stay editable. Agents connected to other tools can also join the same workflow, for example pulling documents from Google Docs, building a design in Adobe's tools, and sharing the result in Slack. These Creative Cloud integrations are not yet available, but Adobe says a private beta will launch in early 2027.

Adobe also previewed "always-on" agents that keep running recurring tasks in the background, so you can work on other things or leave your computer. You give the agent a job, such as organizing incoming files, running ongoing quality checks, or preparing content. You then review its plan and approve the final result. One example is an agent that turns every new image into promotional graphics for different social media channels, letting you pick the best ones to publish each day. Adobe has not said when this preview will launch, but it will come to the Firefly AI Assistant first.

The Firefly AI Assistant beta is also getting upgrades. A Plan Mode lets you review, edit, and approve the agent's plan before it runs a task. A Model Selector lets you choose which AI model to use for a project, or leave it on auto-select so the system picks one based on the result you need. The assistant also now connects with Firefly Boards. You can set preferred formats, colors, brand guidelines, characters, and products, and apply them automatically to every project.

Adobe's creative agent has been built into Premiere, Photoshop, Illustrator, InDesign, After Effects, and Frame.io since it launched earlier this year, and it is now expanding further into video editing. In Premiere, it can track a masked subject through a frame and apply effects or adjust color and exposure across whole clip sequences. The agent is also coming to the Premiere mobile app, so you can make conversational video edits on the go.

Adobe's creativity head, David Wadhwani, said in April that the Adobe creative agent will eventually appear in virtually everything the company develops. Whether Adobe builds its own agents or opens its apps to third-party bots, AI agents are set to play a central role in the company's future.

items.t: Claude Code is accidentally exposing secrets all over GitHub
items.x: "Do not ask again" prompt leads to passwords, API keys, and more being shared.
items.xd:
Security researchers at Apiiro found that Claude Code, an AI coding tool, is accidentally exposing sensitive information in public GitHub repositories. They found thousands of secrets, including database passwords, API tokens, and root logins, inside Claude Code settings files stored in those repositories.

The problem comes from how Claude Code handles approval for automated shell commands. When a user selects "Yes, and don't ask again" to approve a command, that choice is saved as a rule in a local settings file called ".claude/settings.local.json." The command is often saved exactly as written, including any sensitive information it contains.

On a user's own computer, this is generally not a serious issue. Anthropic's documentation says the settings file is added to the developer's global .gitignore list, which usually keeps it from being shared publicly. However, that protection does not carry over to the repository level. If a repository is cloned to another machine, or if a folder later becomes a repository, the file can be uploaded by accident. Apiiro says Claude Code itself will often commit changes to the file without the user's input.

Apiiro's researchers found more than 100,000 cases where the settings file had been uploaded to a public GitHub repository. About 1,100 of these, from 63 different organizations, contained secrets such as public API tokens, database passwords, or private keys. Even after a file is removed from a repository, the secrets can remain in forks of the project if users are not careful.

The issue was first flagged in a Claude Code bug report in August 2025. Other reports noted that the settings file was sometimes not added to .gitignore, or that sensitive commands could be saved to a file without git protection. These reports were closed without action after 60 days of inactivity.

Boris Cherny of the Claude Code team said on Hacker News over the weekend that the team is "looking into what we can do to prevent this." He said these files should almost never be checked into a user's git source control and that such cases seemed to happen only when the files were manually created and checked in. He recommended Claude Code's auto mode, which uses classifiers to handle routine permission prompts without manual allow and deny lists. When another user pointed out that sensitive commands can still be saved to settings files in auto mode, Cherny said the team is working on improving this.

Cherny also recommended that users run secret scanners, tools that search files for sensitive information and remove it. He said the team is considering building similar scanning into Claude Code in the future. However, Apiiro found that 215 of the roughly 1,100 public secrets in these settings files were missed by two popular scanners, gitleaks and TruffleHog.

This is not the only case of an AI agent accidentally leaking sensitive information. Last month, Meta suspended the sharing feature on its Muse agent after security researchers found that its share links could be easily guessed.

items.t: CodeRabbit scales agentic software development and ships 20x more
items.x: CodeRabbit uses OpenAI models to govern and trust AI-generated code and Codex to ship 20 times more software with the same engineering team.
items.xd:
CodeRabbit is a company whose co-founder and CEO, Harjot Gill, says that checking AI-written code is becoming the main job for teams that use coding agents. He says code review is usually the first bottleneck companies hit once they adopt these agents.

The company has built an AI platform to check, govern, and secure code that AI agents produce, and to help teams decide what is ready to release. According to the article, more than 20,000 organizations and over 150,000 open-source projects use it.

CodeRabbit says better price-performance from OpenAI models lets it add more AI agents to its reviews and pass those savings on to customers. It also says Codex helps it ship 20 times more software with the same engineering team. The company uses another OpenAI tool, Daybreak, to secure its own systems and its customers' code.

Its newest product, CodeRabbit Secure, uses Daybreak with Codex models. Its security agents find and fix vulnerabilities.

Gill says each new OpenAI model has greatly improved the product's ability to find problems at scale, especially the reasoning models. CodeRabbit first built its product on GPT-3.5 Turbo. GPT-4 made the product effective at reviewing code, and the company later adopted OpenAI o1 and o3 early. Because reviews run in the cloud without needing real-time responses, the company could use models that took longer to reason through problems in exchange for deeper analysis.

The team tests new models against its own benchmark of known issues. At the time of the interview, Gill estimated that GPT-6 Astra caught 50% of the issues in that dataset, which he said put it at the top among the models tested. The benchmark keeps changing as agents make new kinds of mistakes and as fixes reveal problems that earlier reviews missed.

Lower model prices and caching have let CodeRabbit use more AI in its product. When it started, it used one or two subagents for code navigation. Now, lower-cost models such as GPT-6 Luna run more subagents across the platform, while GPT-6 Astra handles planning and coordination. Gill says the company now uses agents in places it could not afford before, which lets it check more changes and explain them to developers who did not write the code.

Over the last six months, Gill says the company has shipped roughly 20 times more software without adding engineers. He estimates he personally pushed 2,500 to 3,000 pull requests in the 30 days before the interview.

Using Codex required more than just adopting it. Running many agents at once exposed limits in laptop memory, computing power, testing, build tools, and dependencies. The team simplified its release process, rethought where people needed to approve changes, and let CodeRabbit automatically ship low-risk changes that did not need human review. Gill says the whole software delivery process had to be rethought.

The company also built a Codex-powered Slack bot that sorts production incidents, Slack messages, and support tickets, and can return a pull request for the team to review and merge. Gill sees cloud-based development as a way to reduce the limits of local machines and give teams better control over access and auditing.

CodeRabbit also uses Codex for non-engineering work. In marketing, it manages Google Ads through pull requests, opening and merging a request to launch ads. A content studio repository lets Codex create slide decks and customer documents. Gill says turning marketing problems into code problems lets a team move ten times faster.

CodeRabbit has run agents in sandbox environments since 2023, where they clone repositories and write code to help with reviews. More recently, it used OpenAI's Cyber model through Daybreak to test its own platform. The team ran internal penetration tests to look for ways an attacker could break in. Gill says this early access helped the company find several serious vulnerabilities it had not imagined.

The company has since offered these capabilities to customers through CodeRabbit Secure. In a promotion over the past two weeks, it covered $1 million in free deep scans for users. Those scans, all powered by Codex models, found more than 43,000 security vulnerabilities across 13,000 deep scans. Customers have already fixed thousands of them.

As background agents start responding to alerts and incidents without a person starting each task, Gill expects teams to need more help deciding which changes should be finished and shipped.

Looking ahead, CodeRabbit is moving toward agentic software development, helping teams check, prioritize, explain, secure, and verify agent-written code at scale. Gill says the goal is to help developers stay in control as agents do more of the building, with checks, explanations, and upkeep that keep pace with the code being produced.
